analogy.p: Imagine dissolving one big sugar cube and the same mass of fine sugar grains in tea. The grains dissolve much faster because far more sugar is touching the tea at once, just as a nanoparticle exposes far more of its atoms to reacting substances than the same mass of larger particles. This maps to a high surface area to volume ratio. The analogy breaks down because sugar only dissolves, whereas nanoparticles can also have changed optical, electrical and biological properties that ordinary grains do not have.
analogy.t: A tray of sugar cubes versus a bag of sugar grains

bullets: **Nanoparticle**: a particle with a diameter of 1-100 nm (1 x 10^-9 m to 1 x 10^-7 m).
1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m, so 100 nm = 1 x 10^-7 m. Remember the prefix: nano means billionth.
A nanoparticle contains only **a few hundred atoms**, so a large fraction of its atoms are on the surface.
**Bulk material** means a large piece that contains very many atoms, such as a lump or powder of the same substance.
Nanoparticles can be made of metals, metal oxides, carbon (such as fullerenes and nanotubes) and other substances.
**Nanoscience** is the study; **nanotechnology** is using these tiny structures to make useful products.
Link: fullerenes and carbon nanotubes (previous spec point) are examples of nanoscale structures.
core.p: **Nanoscience** is the study of very small structures, which are about **1-100 nanometres (nm)** in size. This is of the order of **a few hundred atoms**. A nanometre is one billionth of a metre, so 1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m. The reason this size range gets its own name is that when a material is divided into pieces this small, its properties can change a lot compared with the same material in big lumps, which scientists call the **bulk** material. That is why a whole branch of science and technology has grown up around it.

bullets: **Fullerenes**: hollow carbon cages (C60 is spherical); used for drug delivery, as lubricants and as catalyst supports.
**Carbon nanotubes**: cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratio; strong, conduct electricity, used in electronics and to reinforce materials.
**Graphene**: one layer of graphite, one atom thick; conducts electricity and is very strong.
All of these have covalent bonding with delocalised electrons in places; link back to the structure and bonding topic.
The size range is the key: a particle must be 1-100 nm in diameter to be called a nanoparticle.
Nanoparticles are not the same as atoms: an atom is about 0.1 nm, so a nanoparticle is made of up to a few hundred atoms.
Quote the **structure** (what it is made of) and the **size** (why it behaves differently) when explaining a property.
core.h: Where nanoscale structures fit with the rest of the topic
core.p: Several structures you have already met are nanoscale, so this topic links directly to the earlier bonding work. **Fullerenes** such as buckminsterfullerene (C60) and **carbon nanotubes** are made of carbon atoms arranged in hexagonal rings and are only a few nanometres across, which makes them nanoparticles. Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, so it is a nanoscale sheet. The reason these are useful comes from their structure and from their size together: strong covalent bonds make them strong, while their tiny size gives a very large surface area compared with their volume. Exam questions often combine the two ideas, for example asking why nanotubes make a good catalyst support or a strong, light material.

bullets: **Coarse particles (PM10)**: diameters between 1 x 10^-5 m and 2.5 x 10^-6 m, that is 2500 nm to 10 000 nm.
**Fine particles (PM2.5)**: diameters between 100 nm and 2500 nm (1 x 10^-7 m to 2.5 x 10^-6 m).
**Nanoparticles**: diameters between 1 nm and 100 nm (1 x 10^-9 m to 1 x 10^-7 m).
An atom is about 0.1 nm across, so a nanoparticle is a few hundred atoms wide or less.
Convert before comparing: to change metres to nm multiply by 10^9; to change nm to metres divide by 10^9.
Example: 3.2 x 10^-7 m = 320 nm, so it is a **fine particle**, not a nanoparticle.
Nanoparticles are the smallest of the three groups, so they have the **largest** surface area to volume ratio.
core.p: You need to be able to compare **coarse particles**, **fine particles** and **nanoparticles** by their diameters. These three groups appear in air-pollution topics as well as in nanoscience, and exam questions often give a diameter and ask you to classify it. The sizes are best remembered in nanometres, because the numbers are then simpler, though the specification quotes some of them in metres. Each group is roughly a hundred times or ten times bigger than the one before, and the smaller the particle the greater the proportion of its atoms exposed at its surface.

bullets: SA:V = surface area / volume (units are for example 1/cm or 1/nm).
For a cube of side L: surface area = 6 x L x L (six square faces) and volume = L x L x L.
So for a cube **SA:V = 6L^2 / L^3 = 6 / L**; the smaller the side, the bigger the ratio.
Worked check: L = 1 cm gives SA 6 cm2, V 1 cm3, ratio 6 per cm. L = 3 cm gives SA 54 cm2, V 27 cm3, ratio 2 per cm.
Surface atoms can react with, or collide with, other particles; atoms inside the particle cannot.
Same idea appears in biology (exchange surfaces, why large organisms need transport systems) and in rates of reaction (powders react faster).
Always say **'per unit of volume'** when you define it; marks are lost for just saying 'larger surface area'.
core.h: Surface area to volume ratio: what it means
core.p: The **surface area to volume ratio** (SA:V) tells you how much surface a particle has for every unit of volume it contains. It is found by dividing the surface area by the volume. A high ratio means a lot of surface for a small amount of material, so a large proportion of the atoms are on the outside where they can touch other substances. This single idea explains almost everything about nanoparticles, so make sure you can explain it clearly in your own words and also calculate it for a cube.

bullets: Cube side 10 nm: SA = 6 x 100 = 600 nm2, V = 1000 nm3, SA:V = 0.6 per nm.
Cube side 100 nm: SA = 6 x 10 000 = 60 000 nm2, V = 1 000 000 nm3, SA:V = 0.06 per nm.
Side divided by 10 (100 nm to 10 nm) means ratio multiplied by 10 (0.06 to 0.6).
Cutting a 3 cm cube into 27 cubes of 1 cm: volume stays 27 cm3 but surface area rises from 54 cm2 to 162 cm2, three times as much.
For the same **mass** of material, nanoparticles expose far more surface than larger particles.
Spheres behave in the same way: surface area to volume ratio = 3 / radius, so it also rises as the radius falls.
The figure of 10 applies to cubes in the exam; do not claim it for every shape without saying so.
core.h: Effect of making the particle smaller: the factor of 10 rule
core.p: The specification says that as the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10, the surface area to volume ratio **increases by a factor of 10**. This follows directly from SA:V = 6/L: if L becomes one tenth as large, 6/L becomes ten times as large. You can show the same effect by cutting a cube into smaller cubes: the total volume stays the same but the total surface area increases because many new faces appear. Examiners like to see a numerical demonstration, so learn at least one example.

bullets: High SA:V means more atoms exposed, so nanoparticles can be **more reactive** than the same substance in bulk.
Nanoparticle catalysts give a much larger surface for reactant particles to collide with and react on.
Optical properties can change: for example zinc oxide and titanium dioxide nanoparticles are transparent on skin, whereas larger particles look white.
Silver nanoparticles are much more effective at killing bacteria than lumps of silver because they expose more silver.
Electrical and mechanical properties can change too, which is why nanotubes are used to strengthen materials.
Always link the difference in properties to **surface area to volume ratio**; do not just say 'they are smaller'.
Typical mark scheme wording: 'nanoparticles have a high surface area to volume ratio so a greater proportion of atoms are available to react'.
core.h: Why nanoparticles have different properties from bulk material
core.p: Nanoparticles often have properties that are **different from the properties of the same materials in bulk**. The main reason is the **very high surface area to volume ratio**, which means that a much larger fraction of the atoms are at the surface and available to react or interact. Surface atoms have fewer neighbouring atoms bonded to them than atoms in the middle, so they behave differently. At this scale there can also be changes in how the material absorbs light, conducts electricity or melts, and these changes are the basis of many uses.

bullets: Catalyst: changes the rate of a reaction and is not used up; it provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.
Reaction takes place on the surface of the catalyst, so more surface means more reactant collisions per second.
Nanoparticle catalysts: **less catalyst needed** for the same effect, which cuts cost (many catalysts are precious metals).
Used in industry, in fuel cells, and in catalytic converters in the exhaust systems of cars.
Some nanostructured catalysts can be more selective, giving more of the useful product and less waste.
Evaluation point: nanoparticle catalysts may be hard to separate from the products and may be lost into the environment.
Link to rates of reaction: increasing surface area increases the frequency of collisions and so the rate.
core.p: A **catalyst** speeds up a reaction without being used up. Reactions on a catalyst happen at its surface, so the more surface that is exposed the faster the reaction goes. Because nanoparticles have a huge surface area to volume ratio, a given mass of nanoparticle catalyst provides far more surface than the same mass of larger particles. This means you can use **smaller quantities** of an often expensive catalyst, such as platinum, and still get the same rate. That lowers costs and saves resources, and some nanoparticle catalysts also work under milder conditions.

bullets: **Drug delivery**: nanoparticles (such as fullerene-based cages) can carry drug molecules to specific cells in the body, so lower doses are needed and side effects may be reduced.
**Silver nanoparticles** are antibacterial, so they are used in wound dressings and in coatings on medical equipment to reduce infection.
Their high surface area lets many drug molecules be attached to one particle.
Nanoparticles are small enough to pass into cells, which can help treatment but also raises safety concerns.
Many nanomedicine treatments are new, so their long term effects on health are not fully known.
Benefit: more targeted treatments; risk: nanoparticles might build up in the body or damage healthy cells.
Make the point that testing and regulation are needed before medical use.
core.p: Nanoparticles are being developed for **medicine**, where their tiny size lets them get into places larger particles cannot and where their large surface area lets many drug molecules be attached. This is called nanomedicine. Some uses are already in everyday healthcare, while others are still being researched, so questions usually ask you to say that some are 'new' or 'being developed'. You need to know a few examples and what makes them useful.

bullets: **Electronics**: smaller circuits, thin conducting coatings and sensors based on nanoparticles and nanotubes.
Nanotubes are strong and light, so they are used in sports equipment such as tennis rackets and in composite materials.
Silver nanoparticles are added to clothing, such as socks, to kill bacteria and reduce smell.
Nanoparticle coatings can make surfaces self-cleaning or scratch-resistant.
Sensors using nanoparticles can detect tiny amounts of a substance because of their high surface area.
Advantage: improved performance from small quantities of material.
Possible disadvantage: nanoparticles can be washed out of fabrics into the water supply.
core.h: Uses in electronics, fabrics and materials
core.p: In **electronics**, nanoscale structures let manufacturers make components smaller and more efficient. Materials such as carbon nanotubes conduct electricity well and are very strong, and nanoparticles can be used in coatings and conducting inks. Because only a small amount of nanomaterial may be needed, products can be lighter and sometimes cheaper to run. Nanoparticles are also added to fabrics and materials to give them new properties, which links to the idea that tiny structures give 'new' properties compared with bulk.

bullets: Sun cream: titanium dioxide and zinc oxide nanoparticles block UV, giving better skin coverage than larger particles.
Nanoparticles in sun cream are **transparent**, so the cream is not visible on the skin.
Deodorants: nanoparticles (often silver) kill the bacteria that cause body odour.
Cosmetics: nanoparticles help give smooth texture and make colours more even.
Benefit: effective protection against UV that can cause skin cancer.
Worry: the particles are small enough that they might be absorbed through the skin or washed into rivers and seas.
A balanced answer mentions both benefit (improved protection) and risk (effects not fully known).
core.h: Uses in cosmetics, sun creams and deodorants
core.p: **Cosmetics, sun creams and deodorants** are the most common everyday examples. In sun creams the nanoparticles of **titanium dioxide and zinc oxide** absorb or scatter harmful ultraviolet radiation, giving better protection and covering the skin evenly, and they are transparent so the cream does not leave a white film. In deodorants, silver nanoparticles act as antibacterial agents. In moisturisers and other cosmetics nanoparticles help ingredients to spread smoothly and to be absorbed. These products are used widely and are applied directly to skin, which is why safety debates focus on them.

bullets: Very small particles may be able to enter the body by being breathed in, swallowed or absorbed through skin, and may enter cells.
Possible harm to health: inhaled nanoparticles might damage lungs or build up in organs.
Long-term effects are **not fully known**, because the technology is new and not enough research has been done.
Possible harm to the environment: nanoparticles washed from clothing or cosmetics may enter water and harm aquatic organisms.
Nanoparticles can be hard to remove from water or air because of their small size.
Possible need for more testing, regulation and labelling so that consumers can make informed choices.
Different people weigh the same evidence differently, so give reasons for any opinion.
core.p: Because nanoparticles are so small they can behave differently inside living things and the environment, and scientists have not finished studying their long-term effects. This is the second half of the specification point: you must be able to **evaluate** uses by weighing benefits against risks. Never claim that nanoparticles are definitely dangerous, since the key point is that the risks are **not fully known**. The word 'possible' or 'may' is what mark schemes expect.

bullets: Start with the **property**: high SA:V so more effective or less material needed.
Then the **benefit**: better UV protection, cheaper catalyst, fewer infections, lighter materials.
Then the **risk**: effects on health and environment are not fully known and the particles can be absorbed or released.
Then a **judgement**: for example 'benefits outweigh risk only if products are tested and regulated'.
Use comparative language such as 'whereas', 'however', 'on the other hand'.
Do not simply list uses; link each to a property.
Higher-mark answers refer to the evidence in the question, for example the size range or the cost data.
core.h: Evaluating uses: structure for 4 and 6 mark answers
core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to 'evaluate', 'discuss' or 'give arguments for and against' the use of nanoparticles in a named product. You should give at least one benefit linked to a property of the nanoparticle, at least one risk linked to size, and then a reasoned conclusion. The conclusion is where the top mark is earned, so make a decision (for example, that more testing is needed before widespread use) and justify it. Use data given in the question where possible, for example mass, price or sizes.

bullets: nm to m: divide by 10^9 (or multiply by 10^-9). Example 80 nm = 8 x 10^-8 m.
m to nm: multiply by 10^9. Example 2.5 x 10^-6 m = 2500 nm.
SA:V of a cube side 5 nm: SA = 6 x 25 = 150 nm2; V = 125 nm3; ratio = 1.2 per nm.
Side 50 nm gives SA 15 000 nm2, V 125 000 nm3, ratio 0.12, ten times smaller than for 5 nm.
Ratio changes by the inverse of the size change (half as long a side gives twice the ratio).
Quote ratios with units (per nm or nm^-1) or as 'x : 1'.
Show the working: marks are usually given for surface area, volume and the division.
core.h: Calculations and standard form with nanoparticles
core.p: Exam questions often involve sizes written in standard form or in nanometres, and ask you to convert, compare or calculate a ratio. Take care with the powers of ten: 1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m, so a particle 25 nm across is 25 x 10^-9 m = 2.5 x 10^-8 m. To compare areas, work with the same units throughout. Check your answer by asking whether a smaller particle really ends up with a larger SA:V.

exam: **State/Name (1 mark)**: give a precise fact, for example 'nanoparticles are 1-100 nm in diameter' or 'titanium dioxide'.
**Define (1-2 marks)**: use the exact wording: 'a few hundred atoms', '1-100 nm', 'surface area to volume ratio'.
**Explain (2-3 marks)**: link three ideas: small size, high SA:V, therefore more atoms available to react (or less catalyst needed).
**Calculate SA:V (3 marks)**: surface area (1), volume (1), divide (1); give units.
**Compare sizes (2 marks)**: convert both to the same unit first, then state which is larger and by what factor.
**Describe use (2 marks)**: name the use and the property that makes it suitable, for example 'silver nanoparticles are antibacterial so are used in wound dressings'.
**Evaluate (4-6 marks)**: benefit, risk, linkage to evidence, and a justified conclusion. Level-based marking rewards a balanced argument.
Useful phrases: 'high surface area to volume ratio', 'not fully known', 'more atoms exposed', 'smaller quantities needed', 'further testing required'.
Command word 'suggest' means apply knowledge to an unfamiliar product (for example nanoparticles in a new paint).
Graph/data tip: if given a table of particle diameters, convert to nm and put them in order before answering.
Use standard form correctly; marks are lost for wrong powers of ten.
Do not use vague words like 'better' or 'stronger' without saying why.

mistakes.r: Atoms are the same size whatever the particle size; nanoparticles are particles of 1-100 nm containing a few hundred atoms.
mistakes.w: Nanoparticles are made of tiny atoms.

mistakes.r: Say a larger surface area to volume ratio (or larger surface area for the same mass); a single nanoparticle has a smaller total surface area than a big lump.
mistakes.w: Nanoparticles have a larger surface area.

mistakes.r: The effects on health and the environment are not fully known; more research and testing are needed. Give a balanced judgement.
mistakes.w: Nanoparticles are dangerous and should be banned.

mistakes.r: 1 nm = 1 x 10^-9 m (1 micrometre is 10^-6 m).
Catalysts are not used up; a smaller mass is needed because nanoparticles have a larger SA:V so more surface is available.
mistakes.w: Catalysts are used up so you need less nanoparticle catalyst.

mistakes.r: Fine particles are 100-2500 nm; nanoparticles are 1-100 nm.
SA is 6L^2 and V is L^3, so SA:V = 6/L; remember six faces.
mistakes.w: The SA:V of a cube is L squared over L.

mistakes.r: It goes up: dividing the side by 10 multiplies the ratio by 10.
mistakes.w: The surface area to volume ratio goes down when the cube gets smaller.

mistakes.r: Nanoparticles are made of the same atoms as the bulk material (e.g. titanium dioxide); only the size and so the properties change.
mistakes.w: Nanoparticles are a new kind of atom or element.

mistakes.r: Evidence is limited: say risks are not fully known, and judge benefits against possible harm to health and the environment.
mistakes.w: Nanoparticles are always harmful or always safe.

summary: You must know that nanoscience studies structures 1-100 nm in size (a few hundred atoms), compare nanoparticles with fine and coarse particles, and explain why very small particles behave differently from the same material in bulk because of their huge surface area to volume ratio. You must also evaluate the uses (medicine, electronics, cosmetics, sun creams, deodorants, catalysts) against the possible risks. This is a triple-only (separate chemistry) topic and a classic source of 4 and 6 mark evaluation questions.

worked.q: A cube-shaped nanoparticle has sides of 5 nm. Calculate its surface area to volume ratio and compare it with a cube of side 50 nm. [4 marks]
steps: Surface area of 5 nm cube = 6 x 5 x 5 = 150 nm2.
50 nm cube: SA = 6 x 2500 = 15 000 nm2; V = 125 000 nm3; ratio = 0.12 per nm.

worked.ans: Nanoparticles of titanium dioxide have a very high surface area to volume ratio, so they cover the skin evenly and absorb UV radiation effectively, giving good protection against skin cancer, and they are transparent so the cream is not visible, which encourages use. However, because they are so small they might be absorbed through the skin or enter cells, and when washed off they could damage aquatic organisms. The long-term effects on health and the environment are not fully known. Overall, the benefits of better protection are significant, but I think more research and regulation are needed before the risk can be judged acceptable.
worked.q: Sun cream contains nanoparticles of titanium dioxide. Evaluate the use of nanoparticles in sun cream. [6 marks]
steps: Property: nanoparticles have a high surface area to volume ratio, so they spread evenly and absorb or scatter UV well.
Benefit 1: better protection against UV radiation that can cause skin cancer.
Benefit 2: the particles are transparent so the cream does not leave a white film, so people are more likely to use it.
Risk 1: the nanoparticles may be absorbed through the skin or enter cells; effects are not fully known.
Risk 2: they may be washed into rivers and seas and harm aquatic life.
Conclusion: benefits are clear but long term risks are not fully known, so more testing and regulation is needed.
